speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our economy has made considerable progress toward both goals over the past two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market has come into better balance, and the unemployment rate remains low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased substantially from a peak of 7 percent to 2.5 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are strongly committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent goal in support of a strong economy that benefits everyone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, the FOMC decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged and to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are maintaining our restrictive stance of monetary policy in order to keep demand in line with supply and reduce inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are attentive to risks on both sides of our dual mandate, and I will have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has continued to expand at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP growth moderated to 2.1 percent in the first half of the year, down from 3.1 percent last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Private domestic final purchases, or PDFP—which excludes inventory investment, government spending, and net exports and usually sends a clearer signal of underlying demand—grew at a 2.6 percent pace over that same period, the first half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Growth of consumer spending has slowed from last year’s robust pace but remains solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Investment in equipment and intangibles has picked up from its anemic pace last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the housing sector, investment stalled in the second quarter after a strong rise in the first.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Improving supply conditions have supported resilient demand and the strong performance of the U.S. economy over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, supply and demand conditions have come into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 177,000 jobs per month in the second quarter—a solid pace, but below that seen in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate has moved up but remains low at 4.1 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Strong job creation over the past couple of years has been accompanied by an increase in the supply of workers, reflecting increases in participation among individuals aged 25 to 54 years and a strong pace of immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has eased over the past year, and the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a broad set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market have returned to about where they stood on the eve of the pandemic—strong, but not overheated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased notably over the past two years but remains somewhat above our longer-run goal of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total PCE prices rose 2.5 percent over the 12 months ending in June; excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.6 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households and businesses and forecasters, as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I are acutely aware that high inflation imposes significant hardship, as it erodes purchasing power, especially for those least able to meet the higher costs of essentials like food, housing, and transportation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of these goals, the Committee decided at today’s meeting to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 5¼ to 5½ percent and to continue reducing our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As the labor market has cooled and inflation has declined, the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals continue to move into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Indeed, we’re attentive to the risks to both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve stated that we do not expect it will be appropriate to reduce the target range for the federal funds rate until we have gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The second quarter’s inflation readings have added to our confidence, and more good data would further strengthen that confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to make our decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that reducing policy restraint too soon or too much could result in a reversal of the progress we have seen on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, reducing policy restraint too late or too little could unduly weaken economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In considering any adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As the economy evolves, monetary policy will adjust in order to best promote our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy remains solid and inflation persists, we can maintain the current target range for the federal funds rate as long as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the labor market were to weaken unexpectedly or inflation were to fall more quickly than anticipated, we are prepared to respond.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to bringing inflation back down to our 2 percent goal and to keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to achieving maximum employment and stable prices over the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So on September, let me say this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we have made no decisions about future meetings, and that includes the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The broad sense of the Committee is that the economy is moving closer to the point at which it will be appropriate to reduce our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In that, we will be data dependent but not data point dependent, so it will not be a question of responding specifically to one or two data releases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The question will be whether the totality of the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks are consistent with rising confidence on inflation and maintaining a solid labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If that test is met, a reduction in our policy rate could be on the table as soon as the next meeting in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would just say, again, that the broad sense of the Committee is that we’re getting closer to the point at which it will be appropriate to reduce our policy rate but that we’re not quite at that point yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I guess I would—I would think about it this way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll give an example of, of cases in which it would be appropriate to cut and maybe that it wouldn’t be appropriate to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if we were to see, for example, inflation moving down quickly or more or less in line with expectations, growth remains, let’s say, reasonably strong, and the labor market remains, you know, consistent with its current condition, then I would think that a, a rate cut could be on the table at the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If, if inflation were to prove, you know, sticky and we were to see higher readings from inflation, disappointing readings, we would weigh that along with the other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think it’s going to be not just any one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s going to be the inflation data, it’s going to be the employment data, it’s going to be the balance of risks as we see it—it’s going to be the totality of all of that that would help us make this decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I think it’s just a question of seeing more good data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have seen—the last couple of readings have, have certainly added to confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve seen progress across all three categories of core PCE inflation—that’s goods, nonhousing services, and housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s really just—you know, we had a quarter of poor inflation data at the beginning of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Then we saw some more good inflation data; we had seven months at the end of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we just want to see more and, and gain confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I said, we have—we did gain confidence, and more good data would cause us to, to gain more confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, so I would just say, really, the path ahead is going to depend on the way the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I can’t really give you any, any better forward guidance on it than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We didn’t, of course, do an SEP at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will do another one at the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would just say, I can—I can imagine a scenario in which there would be everywhere from zero cuts to several cuts, depending on the way the economy evolves, and I wouldn’t want to lay out a baseline path for you there today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve said what I—what I can say about September and about today, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this is the very reason that we’re thinking about—that we’ve said in our—in our statement that we’re going back to looking at both mandates and that we think the risks are coming back into balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think what the data broadly show in the labor market is an ongoing, gradual normalization of labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’ve seen that over a period of a couple of years and a move, really, from overheated conditions to more normal conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are watching the labor market conditions quite closely, and that’s what we’re seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we—if we start to see something that looks to be more than that, then we’re well positioned to respond.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s part of what we’re thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have, we have—growth isn’t one of our three.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have two mandates, as you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market, maximum employment is one, and stable prices is another.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we weigh—we weigh those two things equally under the law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When we were far away from our inflation mandate, we had to focus on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now we’re back, back to a closer to even focus, so we’ll be looking at labor market conditions and asking whether we’re getting what we’re seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I said, we’re prepared to respond if we see that it’s—that it’s not what we wanted to see, which was, you know, a gradual normalization of conditions—if we see more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it wouldn’t be any one statistic, although, of course, the unemployment rate is generally thought to be, you know, a single—a good single statistic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’d be looking at wages, we’d be looking at participation, we’d be looking at all the things—surveys, quits, hires, all of those things—to determine the overall status of the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’re looking at it now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say, again, I think you’re back to conditions that are close to 2019 conditions, and that was not an inflationary economy—broadly similar labor markets then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think inflation was actually—core inflation was actually running below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we don’t think—I don’t now think of the labor market in its current state as a likely source of significant inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would—I would not like to see a material further cooling in the labor market, and that’s part of what’s behind our thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The other part, of course, is that we have made real progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re—we’ve got growing confidence there that we are not quite there yet, but we’re more confident that we’re on a—that we’re on a sustainable path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those two things are working together, and we’re factoring those both into our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t say I wouldn’t want to see any other cooling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It would be more of a material difference.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we—if we’d be looking at this and if we see something that looks like a more significant downturn, that would be something that we would—we would have the intention of responding to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, in terms of—I don’t think of it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think of it as, you know, we’re actually in a good place here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re balancing these two risks of, you know, go too soon, and you undermine progress on inflation; wait too long or don’t go fast enough, and, and you put at risk the recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we have to balance those two things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the nature of having two mandates, and I think we—this is how we balance them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a rough balance, but it does feel like, again, the labor market feels like it’s in a place where it’s just a process of ongoing normalization; 4.1 percent unemployment is still historically low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’ll just have to see what the data show us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think all of the data points continue to point to kind of the direction we would want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that was taken as, you know, there was a decline in job openings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That was good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today’s ECI reading was a little softer than expected, so that’s, that’s a good reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It shows that wage increases are still at a strong level but that that level continues to come down to more sustainable levels over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s exactly the pattern that we want to be seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think the data—the data we’ve been seeing in the labor market are broadly consistent with that normalization process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, we’re closely monitoring to see whether it starts to show signs that it’s more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, I can’t really say that, honestly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think it’s just normalization, but we want to be in a position to, to support the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, we’re seeing progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we actually got to this—we raised rates a year ago at the July meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if you look at the situation in the economy a year ago, unemployment—sorry, inflation was over 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was a completely different economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now we’ve made a lot of progress, and the labor market—I think unemployment was in the 3s, mid-3s, so it’s a different economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think it’s time, it’s coming to be time, to adjust that so that we support this continued process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The thing we’re trying to do is—you know that we have, we’ve had this really significant decline in inflation, and unemployment has remained low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is a really unusual and historically, historically unusual and such a welcome outcome for the people we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is—this is part of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think we don’t need to be 100 percent focused on inflation because of the progress we’ve made: 12-month headline at 2½ [percent], core at 2.6.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s way down from where it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The job is not done on inflation, but, nonetheless, we can afford to begin to dial back the restriction in our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think we’re just—it’s part of a process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of what that looks like, I mean, I think most rate—you would think, in a base case, that policy rates would move down from here, but I don’t want to try to give specific forward guidance about when that might be, the pace at which it might happen, because I think that’s really going to depend on the economy, and that’s highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Actually, what we’re seeing now is a little better than what we saw last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Last year, as we pointed out late in the year, a whole lot of the progress we saw last year was from goods prices, which were going down at an unsustainable rate, disinflating at an unsustainable rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is a broader disinflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This has goods prices coming down, but it’s also—we’re also now seeing progress in the other two big categories: nonhousing services and housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, the thing is, we’ve only—you’ve got one quarter of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had seven months of low inflation; you got one quarter of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say the quality of this is, is higher, and it’s good, but so far, it’s only a quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think, you know, we need to see more to know that we’re—to have more confidence that we’re on, on a good path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But as I mentioned, our confidence is growing because we’ve been getting good data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And things like the ECI report and, frankly, the softening in the labor market conditions, you know, give you more confidence that the economy’s not overheating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t look like an overheating economy, and it looks like an economy that’s normalizing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the thing about—if what it is is seasonality, and it could just be—it’s very, very hard to, you know, to do appropriate seasonal adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If that’s what it is, then that actually implies that, that other months were underreporting too low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you smoothed it out, it’s a zero-sum game.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s why we look at 12 months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We look at 12 months because that takes all of that out, all those effects out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Twelve-month now is 2½ percent headline, 2.6 percent core.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is so much better than where we were even a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a lot better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, the job is not done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I want to stress that, and we’re committed to getting the job—inflation sustainably under 2 percent, but we need to take note of that progress, and we need to weigh the risks to the labor market and the risks to our inflation target now more equally than we did a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I—you know, I think that we’ve been given an assignment by Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so in our, you know, quasi-constitutional document, the Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, we look at the two goals, and if one of them is farther away than the other—the two variables, inflation and employment—if one is farther away from its goal than the other, then you, you concentrate on the one that’s farther away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you take account of the time to reach the goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, for the last couple of years, the best service we could do to the American people was to focus on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But as inflation has come down—and I think the upside risks to inflation have decreased as the labor market has cooled off, and now the labor market has softened—you know, probably the inflation, inflation’s probably a little farther from its target than is employment, but I think the downside risks to, to the employment mandate are, are real now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have to weigh all that, and if you think about where that takes us is we have a restrictive policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s clearly restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been the rate we’ve had in place for a full year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the time is coming—as other central banks around the world are facing the same question—the time is coming at which it will begin to be appropriate to dial back that level of restrictions, restriction so that we may address both mandates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: “Certainty” is not a word that we have in our—in our business.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we get—we get a lot of data between now and September, and it isn’t going to be one data read or even two.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s going to be the assessment that we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, we’ll, we’ll all look carefully at the employment report, but so much other data coming in and so much happening between now and the September meeting, and we’ll, you know, we’ll make a judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, you know, we’ll look at everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve seen some, some tendency to have a narrowing base of job creation in some months going back, but then we’ve had some months where, where job creation was broader.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also, you know, the headline number of jobs has come down, so—but you look at the whole thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think you do look at private demand extra carefully, to your point about, about government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll just be looking at, at all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s the risk of going too soon and the risk of going too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve been—you know, we, we had seven months of good inflation data at the end of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We said we wanted to see more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We said—we pointed out that too much of this was coming from goods, and, sure enough, the first quarter wasn’t, wasn’t great—inflation data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And now we’ve got another quarter—a quarter that is good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’re balancing the risk of going too soon against the risk of going too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’re doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s no guarantee in this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a very difficult judgment call, but this is—this is how we’re making it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—but in terms of today, your question about today, we did have a—you know, we had a nice conversation about, about this issue today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The overall sense of the Committee, as I mentioned, is that we’re getting closer to the point at which it will be appropriate to begin to dial back restriction, but we’re not quite at that point yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want to see more good data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The decision was unanimous—all 19 participants supported it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But there was a real discussion back and forth of what the case would be for, for moving at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A strong majority supported moving—not moving at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That was the strong sense of the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s a conversation that we had today, certainly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes, it does.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think the lags have kind of showed up here in the last six months, by the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You, you really do now see the restriction, whereas, I mean, even a few months ago, people were questioning how restrictive policy was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Look at the labor market now—you can see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And look at inflation—sorry—rate-sensitive, interest-sensitive spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You really do see now that policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say it’s extremely restrictive, but it’s certainly effectively restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes, there—the lag should, should be on the way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It should take some time to get into—to get into the full economy, affect financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that affects economic activity, hiring and that kind of thing, and, ultimately, inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t—it’s not instantaneous, although it’s faster than it used to be because markets move now in anticipation of our moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have to worry about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, we—just to make it clear, you know, it’s a very difficult, challenging judgment, and we don’t want to go too soon, and we don’t want to go too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s—this is how we made that judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I feel good about where we are.
